issues.legal_issue: An executing court may examine whether a decree is void for lack of inherent jurisdiction and refuse to execute it if it is a nullity.
material_facts: A party sought execution of a final eviction decree.
The opposing party objected that the decree was void because the court that passed it lacked inherent jurisdiction.
The objection arose after a retrospective amendment made the rent-control law applicable to the tenancy.
issues.conclusion: The executing court was competent to examine whether the decree was a nullity and, if so, to refuse execution.
issues.legal_principle: Although an executing court generally cannot go behind a decree or question its legality or correctness, it may consider an objection that the decree is a nullity for lack of inherent jurisdiction. The Court followed Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan, [1955] 1 SCR 117, and Seth Hiralal Patni v. Sri Kali Nath, [1962] 2 SCR 747.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party sought to enforce a court decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.decree_lacks_inherent_jurisdiction: The court that passed the decree lacked inherent jurisdiction over the case.

issues.definition: When a party seeks to enforce a decree and the court that passed it lacked inherent jurisdiction, the executing court may refuse execution.

issues.legal_issue: A retrospective amendment extending rent-control protection to government premises lawfully let by a person can render an earlier eviction decree void despite its finality.
material_facts: The premises remained government property when they were lawfully let to a tenant by a person who had acquired possession after a public auction.
A civil court passed an eviction decree, and the decree became final before the rent-control law was amended.
The amendment applied retrospectively to government premises lawfully let by any person and expressly applied notwithstanding any judgment, decree, or order.
The tenant objected to execution on the ground that the retrospective amendment deprived the civil court of jurisdiction over the eviction suit.
issues.conclusion: The retrospective proviso had to be treated as part of the law from its enactment; the rent-control law therefore applied to the tenancy, the civil court lacked inherent jurisdiction, and the eviction decree was a nullity that could not be executed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, as amended by the retrospective proviso added by Act 4 of 1963, the Act applied to a tenancy of government premises lawfully let by any person, notwithstanding any judgment, decree, or order. Section 50 excluded the civil court's jurisdiction over eviction matters covered by the Act. A legal fiction created by retrospective legislation must be carried to its logical consequences, as explained in East End Dwellings Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council, [1952] A.C. 132; the express reference to judgments, decrees, and orders showed that their finality did not prevent application of the amendment.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and government_owned_premises and lawfully_let_by_person and retroactive_rent_protection_overrides_judgments

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party sought to enforce an eviction decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.government_owned_premises: The premises remained the property of the government when they were let to the tenant.
predicates.lawfully_let_by_person: A person lawfully let the premises to the tenant.
predicates.retroactive_rent_protection_overrides_ju: A later amendment was made retrospective, extended rent-control protection to government premises lawfully let by a person, and applied notwithstanding judgments, decrees, or orders.

issues.definition: If an eviction decree is being enforced for government premises lawfully let by a person and a retrospective rent-protection rule covers that tenancy notwithstanding judgments, the decree is a nullity.
